9-1.title: Do not share unverified disaster, epidemic or police messages; do not doctor images or use AI to invent a scene
9-1.inPlainWords: Sharing a message you know to be false can make you liable even if you did not create it. Indian law punishes false information that causes public alarm, mischief or hatred under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, while the Information Technology Act, 2000 covers obscene electronic content and identity misuse; a doctored image or an AI-generated scene counts as content you created or spread. Check the official handle or the district administration before forwarding. 'I only shared it' is not a defence.
9-1.benefit: The BNS, 2023 contains the offences for public mischief, false information causing alarm, and defamation; the IT Act, 2000 covers obscene electronic content, identity misuse and the blocking of unlawful material, but it does not create a separate offence of publishing false news. Penalties range from fines to imprisonment, depending on the harm. The Supreme Court and the Election Commission have repeatedly asked platforms and users not to spread unverified claims during disasters and elections. A photoshopped image or an AI-generated video is treated as content, not as a harmless joke, if it causes panic or harm.
9-1.cost: No cost. Check the official district administration, police or health department account before sharing. If you cannot find the source, do not forward it. Do not edit an image to make it more dramatic.
9-1.caveats: Satire and criticism are not automatically offences, but a false factual claim that causes panic can be. The exact offence depends on the words, the audience and the harm. Do not name a suspect or a victim in a forwarded message.
9-1.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000 (sections 66C, 66D, 67). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

9-2.title: Do not insult national symbols or defame anyone online: a group chat is not the private aside it feels like
9-2.inPlainWords: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 punishes insulting the national flag or the Constitution and disrupting the national anthem, and the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950 restricts commercial use of national emblems. Defamation under the BNS, 2023 protects a living person's reputation. India has no rule that makes a group chat 'a public place', but posting to a group is publication to other people, which is exactly what defamation needs. Criticising the government or the armed forces is lawful.
9-2.benefit: Section 2 of the 1971 Act covers insulting the national flag or the Constitution and section 3 covers preventing or disrupting the anthem; the punishment can extend to three years, or a fine, or both. The 1950 Act restricts the use of emblems and names for trade. Defamation under the BNS, 2023 requires a false imputation published to harm a reputation, and the IT Act, 2000 covers obscene publication online. The Supreme Court has protected criticism of the government while upholding action against abuse of national symbols. A dead person cannot be defamed in the technical sense, so posts about a soldier who has died are met with obscenity, public-order and platform rules rather than a martyrs law.
9-2.cost: No cost. Do not forward an edited flag or anthem video, and do not join a pile-on against a named person. Keep the original post if you want to report it.
9-2.caveats: India has no statute that specially protects the reputation of martyrs; the routes that exist are the 1971 Act, defamation of a living person, obscenity, and the platform's own rules. Satire is not automatically safe, and an apology does not end a prosecution. The line depends on the words, the audience and the harm. Keep the evidence before you report a post.
9-2.sources: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Home Affairs. <https://www.mha.gov.in/>

9-3.title: Reading a foreign website is not an offence; sharing material that threatens national security can be
9-3.inPlainWords: India does not criminalise merely reading a foreign website. What can be an offence is possessing or distributing material that promotes terrorism, or acts against the sovereignty and integrity of India. The BNS, 2023 and the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 cover such acts, and the IT Act covers electronic communication. Close the page, do not screenshot or forward, and do not accept money to post political content.
9-3.benefit: Chapter VII of the BNS, 2023 deals with offences against the State, including waging war, sedition-type acts and promoting enmity. The UAPA, 1967 deals with unlawful and terrorist organisations; membership or support can be an offence. The IT Act, 2000 includes provisions on unauthorised access and content. Reading is not the offence; possession with intent, distribution, funding or collaboration is. Penalties can be substantial, including long imprisonment.
9-3.cost: No cost. Close the page. Do not archive, screenshot or share the material, and do not accept payment from an unknown foreign entity to post content.
9-3.caveats: This is a difficult area and the facts matter. A journalist, researcher or human-rights worker may have lawful grounds to hold material. Take a lawyer's advice before publishing or sharing. Do not assume that a foreign server makes the act immune from Indian law.
9-3.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Chapter VII). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

9-4.title: Private viewing is not an offence; posting, selling or running a sharing group is
9-4.inPlainWords: Indian law does not punish watching obscene material in private. It does punish publishing, transmitting or selling it. Under the BNS, 2023 and the IT Act, 2000, distributing obscene material electronically can lead to imprisonment and a fine, and child sexual abuse material is governed by the POCSO Act, 2012 and the IT Act. Do not forward it, do not run a group for it, and never involve a minor.
9-4.benefit: The BNS, 2023 contains offences for selling, distributing or exhibiting obscene material, with higher penalties for a minor. The IT Act, 2000, section 67, punishes publishing or transmitting obscene material in electronic form. The POCSO Act, 2012 punishes the production, distribution and possession of child sexual abuse material. A group admin who allows such material can be treated as a distributor. The offence is distribution, not private viewing.
9-4.cost: No cost. Do not forward, save to a group folder, or become the admin of such a group. Report child sexual abuse material to the police or the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal.
9-4.caveats: The definition of obscenity is judged by community standards and the context. A private group with a few friends can still be a publication if the material is shared. If a minor is involved, the POCSO Act applies regardless of consent.
9-4.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000 (section 67). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>

9-5.title: Never lend your bank account or card for a 'part-time' payment job — it is a money-mule route
9-5.inPlainWords: If someone asks you to receive money in your account and withdraw or transfer it for a commission, you may be helping launder criminal proceeds. Indian banks and the RBI require KYC, and the BNS, 2023 and the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 punish knowingly receiving or concealing the proceeds of crime. A small fee is not worth a frozen account and a criminal case.
9-5.benefit: The BNS, 2023 contains offences for dishonestly receiving stolen property and for cheating. The PMLA, 2002 allows attachment and prosecution for money laundering, and the IT Act covers cyber fraud. Banks freeze accounts flagged for mule activity, and the account holder may face a police case even if the amount was small. The RBI's KYC master directions require banks to monitor such accounts. A 'commission' is evidence of knowledge.
9-5.cost: No cost. Refuse the offer, do not share your card, PIN, OTP or net-banking credentials, and report the recruiter to the bank and on 1930.
9-5.caveats: The fact that you did not know the source is not a complete defence where the pattern was obviously suspicious. A single transaction can trigger a freeze. If your account is frozen, contact the bank and the cyber police rather than trying to move the money.
9-5.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, KYC Master Directions. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>

9-6.title: Never 'package' a loan applicant for a commission — the borrower's name carries the debt and the fraud case
9-6.inPlainWords: A loan is approved on the documents and the borrower's ability to repay. If you help someone use a borrowed identity, fake income or a fake business to get a loan, you may be part of a cheating offence under the BNS, 2023 and a banking fraud. The person whose name is on the loan is liable to repay, and a commission does not transfer that liability.
9-6.benefit: The BNS, 2023 covers cheating, forgery and using a forged document. The RBI and banks treat a loan obtained on false documents as fraud, and the account can be recalled. The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 can apply to the proceeds. A 'commission agent' who arranges the documents can be prosecuted along with the borrower. The credit record of the named borrower is damaged even if someone else took the money.
9-6.cost: No cost. Do not lend your ID, PAN, Aadhaar or bank statement to an agent, and do not sign a loan document you have not read. If an offer depends on a fake salary slip or a fake GST return, walk away.
9-6.caveats: A genuine loan facilitator can help with the paperwork, but must not invent facts. Check the lender's registration and the fees in writing. A loan against a forged document can be recovered from the borrower and the guarantor.
9-6.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, fair practices code. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

9-7.title: Return found property; keeping it or using a found card can be a criminal offence
9-7.inPlainWords: If you find a phone, wallet or cash, try to return it or hand it to the police. Keeping it dishonestly can be an offence under the BNS, 2023, and using a found debit or credit card is treated as cheating or forgery. There is no reward for keeping it, and a finder cannot claim it against the true owner.
9-7.benefit: The BNS, 2023 contains offences for dishonest misappropriation of property and for cheating. The Indian Contract Act, 1872 and the law of torts can require the finder to return the property or compensate the owner. Using a found card at an ATM or online is a separate offence and can lead to a police case without the owner's complaint. A bank will reverse the transaction and may freeze the account.
9-7.cost: No cost. Hand the item to the nearest police station and get a receipt. If it is a phone, answer it and arrange the return. Do not try the card.
9-7.caveats: The exact offence depends on the value and the intention. A found item handed to the police is not yours to keep. A reward offered by the owner is a matter for the owner; it is not a legal right.
9-7.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Indian Contract Act, 1872. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Reserve Bank of India, card safety. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>

9-8.title: Use your real identity for an offer; fake accounts and invented orders are fraud
9-8.inPlainWords: Using one real account to take a genuine discount is fine. Creating fake accounts, fake orders or fake reviews to extract more coupons is cheating, and it can be prosecuted under the BNS, 2023 and the IT Act, 2000. Platforms can also freeze the account and recover the discount. Buying phone numbers or verification codes is a separate offence.
9-8.benefit: The BNS, 2023 covers cheating and forgery; the IT Act, 2000 covers identity theft and cheating by personation. The DPDP Act, 2023 protects personal data, and buying or selling phone numbers or OTPs can violate it. A platform can ban the account and recover the amount. The amount matters for the sentence, but the false identity is the core of the offence.
9-8.cost: No cost. Use your own account and read the offer's one-per-customer rule. Do not join a 'coupon-hunting' group that uses fake numbers or accounts.
9-8.caveats: A genuine pricing error is not your fraud, but exploiting a known loophole repeatedly can be. Keep the offer terms and the receipts. If a platform blocks your account, use its grievance route rather than opening a new fake account.
9-8.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000 (sections 66C, 66D). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

9-9.title: Never throw anything from a balcony or window — a falling object can kill and the liability is personal
9-9.inPlainWords: Throwing a bottle, a cigarette butt or a bag from a height is dangerous and can be a criminal offence if it endangers life or causes hurt. The BNS, 2023 covers acts endangering life and causing hurt, and the law of torts makes the thrower liable for damage. In a flat, the residents' association and the owner can also be liable if the source cannot be identified. Use the bin, not the window.
9-9.benefit: The BNS, 2023 contains offences for rash or negligent acts endangering human life and for causing hurt or death. A civil suit for negligence can award damages. Municipal solid-waste rules prohibit throwing waste from a height. If the object falls from a flat and the thrower cannot be identified, the apartment owners' association and the occupants may face a claim, which is why many societies install cameras.
9-9.cost: No cost. Keep a covered bin on the balcony and use the building's waste collection. Do not flick a cigarette butt.
9-9.caveats: The offence depends on the risk and the harm. A dropped object during shifting is still a risk; warn people below and use a rope or a lift. Report a repeated thrower to the society and the police.
9-9.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, solid waste rules. <https://mohua.gov.in/>

9-10.title: Do not buy an imitation or air gun without checking the Arms Act — 'toy' is not a legal category
9-10.inPlainWords: The Arms Act, 1959 regulates the manufacture, sale, possession and carrying of firearms, including many air guns and imitation firearms. A licence is needed for a category that the Act and the rules cover, and a prohibited arm cannot be kept at all. Buying online does not avoid the Act. If you want to shoot, use a licensed range.
9-10.benefit: The Arms Act, 1959 and the Arms Rules, 2016 set the categories and the licensing process. Unauthorised possession can lead to imprisonment and a fine, and a prohibited weapon attracts a heavier penalty. The police can seize the item and register a case. The fact that a seller calls it a 'toy' or a 'replica' does not decide its legal category.
9-10.cost: No cost. Check the Arms Rules and ask the local licensing authority before buying. A licensed shooting range is the safe route for sport.
9-10.caveats: The classification depends on the weapon's characteristics and the notification in force. State rules may add restrictions. Do not carry a replica in public; it can be treated as a threat even if it cannot fire.
9-10.sources: Arms Act, 1959. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Home Affairs, Arms Rules. <https://www.mha.gov.in/>

9-11.title: Register the drone and stay out of no-fly zones; do not tamper with the altitude limit
9-11.inPlainWords: India's Drone Rules, 2021 require a drone to be registered on the Digital Sky platform, and the remote pilot needs a valid permit where the rules require one. Flying near an airport, a military area or a protected zone is restricted, and tampering with the altitude or geo-fencing can lead to seizure and prosecution under the Aircraft Act, 1934. Register first, check the zone, and keep the drone in sight.
9-11.benefit: The Drone Rules, 2021 set the registration, remote-pilot and airspace requirements, and the Digital Sky platform shows the green, yellow and red zones. The Aircraft Act, 1934 and the rules provide for penalties, including imprisonment and fine, for unauthorised flight or endangering aircraft. The BNS, 2023 can apply where a flight endangers life or property. A drone flown in a no-fly zone can be intercepted or seized.
9-11.cost: Registration and the remote-pilot requirements involve fees, and a drone with the required equipment costs more. Checking the zone on Digital Sky before each flight costs nothing.
9-11.caveats: The rules depend on the drone's weight category and the zone. A micro drone has fewer requirements, but no-fly zones still apply. Do not fly over a crowd or a private property without permission.
9-11.sources: Directorate General of Civil Aviation, Drone Rules 2021. <https://www.dgca.gov.in/>; Digital Sky. <https://digitalsky.dgca.gov.in/>; Aircraft Act, 1934. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

9-12.title: Do not film anyone secretly, and never install a camera in a rented room, homestay or hotel
9-12.inPlainWords: Secretly watching or filming a person in a private place is voyeurism under the BNS, 2023, and can lead to imprisonment and a fine. Installing a hidden camera in a hotel or homestay room, or in a rented flat used by someone else, is an aggravated offence. Distributing the footage adds offences under the IT Act and the obscenity provisions. A camera in your own home is lawful only where it does not capture a guest or tenant in a private space.
9-12.benefit: Section 77 of the BNS, 2023 punishes voyeurism, and section 78 punishes stalking. The IT Act, 2000 covers capturing and publishing private images. The DPDP Act, 2023 restricts processing personal data without consent. The punishment increases where the victim is a woman or a child, and child sexual abuse material falls under POCSO. A hotel or landlord who knowingly allows a hidden camera can also be liable.
9-12.cost: No cost. Do not buy a hidden camera. If you rent a room, check for unusual devices and report a suspected camera to the police and the platform.
9-12.caveats: A camera at your own door for security is different from a camera in a bedroom or bathroom. A guest's consent does not cover a hidden camera in a private space. Preserve the device and the footage if you find one; do not share it online.
9-12.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (sections 77, 78). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal. <https://cybercrime.gov.in/>

9-13.title: A friendly low-stakes card game is fine; a rake, a paid game or online real-money betting is not
9-13.inPlainWords: Playing a low-stakes game of cards with friends is not the target of the gambling laws. Taking a commission from the pot, running a paid game, or operating an online real-money game is. State gambling laws and the Public Gambling Act, 1867 punish keeping a gaming house and wagering; the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 prohibits online money games. Skill games are treated differently, but the line depends on the game and the state.
9-13.benefit: The Public Gambling Act, 1867 and the state gambling statutes punish keeping or being found in a common gaming house. The 2025 online gaming Act prohibits online real-money games and provides penalties for the operator and the promoter. A game of mere skill is outside some state gambling laws, but a rake or a payment to enter can change the character. A payment app or a UPI transfer is evidence of the stake.
9-13.cost: No cost to play a small game at home. Do not pay an entry fee, do not take a cut and do not act as the banker for a group.
9-13.caveats: The state law differs; what is a lawful skill game in one state may be restricted in another. Online platforms may claim a skill exemption that does not cover real-money play. Do not use a friend's account to route the stake.
9-13.sources: Public Gambling Act, 1867. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025. <https://www.meity.gov.in/>; state gambling laws (check your state). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

9-14.title: Do not eat wild animals or keep a protected species as a pet; the Wild Life Act applies
9-14.inPlainWords: The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 protects scheduled animals and plants and regulates trade in them. Hunting, buying, selling or keeping a protected animal without a permit is an offence, and the penalties can include imprisonment and a fine. A pet shop that cannot show the legal source is a risk. Do not rely on a claim that an animal was 'captive-bred' unless the paperwork supports it.
9-14.benefit: The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 schedules the protected species and prohibits their hunting, trade and possession without a permit. The penalties were increased in 2022, and a repeat offence can lead to longer imprisonment. India is also a party to CITES, which restricts international trade in listed species. The BNS, 2023 contains offences for cruelty to animals. A protected species kept as a pet can be seized, and the owner prosecuted.
9-14.cost: No cost to avoid it. Before buying an exotic pet, ask for the source, the permit and the species identification. If the seller cannot provide them, walk away.
9-14.caveats: The list of protected species is long and includes many birds, reptiles and mammals. A 'farm-bred' claim does not override the Act. State forest department rules may add restrictions. Do not release a pet into the wild.
9-14.sources: Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. <https://moef.gov.in/>; CITES. <https://cites.org/>

9-15.title: You cannot detain or confine a debtor; use the court, not the room
9-15.inPlainWords: However genuine the debt, you cannot lock a person in, restrain them, or follow them home and refuse to leave. Doing so can be wrongful confinement and criminal intimidation under the BNS, 2023, and a civil wrong. Recover the money through a court suit, an arbitration clause or, where the amount is small, the small causes court. A debt does not create a right to take the law into your hands.
9-15.benefit: The BNS, 2023 contains offences for wrongful confinement, criminal intimidation and trespass. A civil suit for recovery can be filed in the appropriate court, and an unpaid cheque can support a complaint under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 provides a route where the debtor is insolvent. Self-help recovery can turn a creditor into an accused.
9-15.cost: Court fees and a lawyer cost money, but far less than a criminal case. A written loan agreement, a cheque and a payment trail make recovery easier.
9-15.caveats: A threat of criminal action to recover a debt can itself be extortion if it goes beyond a lawful notice. Do not publish the debtor's name and photo to shame them; that can be defamation. Take legal advice before sending a notice.
9-15.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. <https://ibbi.gov.in/>

9-16.title: Do not lend your ID, Aadhaar or PAN, and do not use someone else's
9-16.inPlainWords: Your Aadhaar, PAN, passport and voter card identify you. Lending them, or using someone else's to open an account, buy a ticket or register a company, can be forgery, cheating or identity theft under the BNS, 2023 and the IT Act, 2000. The Aadhaar Act, 2016 restricts the use and sharing of Aadhaar data. If a copy is required, write the purpose on it and keep the transaction record.
9-16.benefit: The Aadhaar Act, 2016 provides penalties for unauthorised use and disclosure of Aadhaar information. The BNS, 2023 covers forgery, cheating and personation, and the IT Act, 2000 covers identity theft. A company or bank account opened in your name by someone else can create tax and criminal liability for you. The DPDP Act, 2023 gives you rights over your personal data, but it does not excuse lending it.
9-16.cost: No cost. Refuse the request. If you must share a copy, write 'for KYC with X bank, date' across it and keep a copy.
9-16.caveats: A family member asking for your Aadhaar OTP is still asking you to authorise access. Do not share an OTP, even with a caller who claims to be from the bank. If your identity is misused, file a police complaint and inform the bank and the tax department.
9-16.sources: Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and Other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

9-17.title: Stay calm when the police stop you; argue later, not with your hands
9-17.inPlainWords: If the police stop or detain you, comply with a lawful instruction and ask for the grounds. Pushing, hitting or grabbing an officer can be obstructing a public servant or assault under the BNS, 2023, and it turns a complaint into a criminal case. You can record the interaction where the law allows, note the officer's name and badge, and complain afterwards to the senior officer, the State Human Rights Commission or the courts.
9-17.benefit: The BNS, 2023 contains offences for obstructing a public servant and for assault. The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 sets the procedure for arrest, including the right to be informed of the grounds and to consult a lawyer. A person who is arrested must be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours. The police complaints authority and the State Human Rights Commission can examine misconduct. A calm record is stronger evidence than a scuffle.
9-17.cost: No cost. Keep a lawyer's number and a family contact. If you are detained, ask for the grounds and the place of detention, and do not sign a blank document.
9-17.caveats: Do not resist even an unlawful arrest; challenge it afterwards. A bystanding video can help, but do not obstruct the officer to take it. If you are injured, ask for a medical examination and record it.
9-17.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Human Rights Commission. <https://nhrc.nic.in/>

9-18.title: Sexual relations with anyone under 18 are illegal; consent is not a defence
9-18.inPlainWords: In India, the age of consent is 18. The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 treats sexual contact with a person under 18 as an offence, whatever the child says or however mature they look. The BNS, 2023 also punishes rape and sexual assault. A mistaken belief about age is not a defence in law. If you are unsure, do not proceed.
9-18.benefit: The POCSO Act, 2012 defines a child as a person under 18 and punishes sexual assault, sexual harassment and the use of a child for pornographic purposes. The BNS, 2023 punishes rape and sexual assault. The POCSO Act requires mandatory reporting of an offence and provides child-friendly procedures. A marriage of a child is also prohibited under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006. The punishment can be a long prison term.
9-18.cost: No cost. If you are unsure of the person's age, stop. Do not rely on a dating app's age field.
9-18.caveats: The law does not create a general 'close-in-age' exception; a case is decided on its facts, and courts have quashed some consensual cases involving older adolescents, but that is not a rule you can rely on. A school, hospital or public servant who fails to report an offence can be liable under POCSO.
9-18.sources: Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

9-19.title: Do the arithmetic before you hit someone: hurt, compensation and a criminal record
9-19.inPlainWords: A punch can lead to a police case for hurt or grievous hurt under the BNS, 2023, and to a civil claim for medical costs, lost wages and pain. If the injury is simple, the court can impose imprisonment or a fine; if it is grievous, the sentence is longer. A settlement with the victim does not automatically end a criminal case. The few seconds of temper can cost years.
9-19.benefit: The BNS, 2023 contains offences for voluntarily causing hurt (section 115), grievous hurt (section 117) and hurt by a dangerous weapon (section 118). The court can order compensation under the BNSS, 2023 and the civil court can award damages. The amount depends on the medical evidence and the victim's loss. A repeat offence or a group attack attracts a heavier penalty. Self-defence is a defence only where the force is proportionate and necessary.
9-19.cost: No cost to walk away. A lawyer, a medical bill and a settlement cost far more. If you are attacked, call 112 and get a medical examination.
9-19.caveats: A single blow can cause a fatal injury. 'He hit me first' is not a licence to keep hitting; the right of private defence ends when the threat ends. Do not post about the fight online; it becomes evidence.
9-19.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Home Affairs. <https://www.mha.gov.in/>

9-20.title: If you cannot care for a newborn, use the legal adoption route through CARA and pay only the prescribed fee
9-20.inPlainWords: A legal adoption in India runs through the Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 and the Adoption Regulations, 2022. CARA's published guidance states that prospective adoptive parents pay the prescribed adoption fee in instalments, so the process is not free; the fee is for the process, not for the child. A private handover, especially for money, can be prosecuted as trafficking or as a sale of a child, and abandoning a newborn is an offence.
9-20.benefit: The JJ Act, 2015 requires a child in need of care and protection to be produced before the Child Welfare Committee and an adoption to be arranged through CARA and its authorised agencies; an adoption outside that route is not legally recognised. The Adoption Regulations, 2022 set the procedure, the home study and the fee schedule. The BNS, 2023 punishes trafficking, the sale of a child and the abandonment of a young child. Money paid to a parent or a broker is evidence of trafficking, not of adoption.
9-20.cost: The process has a prescribed fee, payable in instalments, and a registered agency may also charge for the child's care. Budget for travel and documents. Never pay an intermediary, and never pay a parent.
9-20.caveats: A hospital or a nursing home cannot arrange a private adoption, and a 'gift' or 'donation' to the mother changes the character of the act. The child's best interest is the legal test, and the biological parent's consent is recorded before the Committee. If you are in crisis after the birth, speak to the hospital social worker, call Childline on 1098, or call Tele-MANAS on 14416 for mental-health support.
9-20.sources: Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Central Adoption Resource Authority. <https://cara.wcd.gov.in/>; Adoption Regulations, 2022. <https://cara.wcd.gov.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Tele-MANAS. <https://telemanas.mohfw.gov.in/>

9-21.title: Do not stage an accident or inflate a claim: insurance fraud is a crime, and the appraiser or garage that helps is liable too
9-21.inPlainWords: Inventing an accident, exaggerating damage or claiming for an old injury is fraud. Under the BNS, 2023 and the Insurance Act, 1938, a false claim can lead to a police case, and the insurer can cancel the policy, refuse the claim and recover money already paid. A surveyor, garage or doctor who certifies a false claim can be prosecuted as an accomplice. The small extra payout is not worth a criminal record.
9-21.benefit: The BNS, 2023 contains offences for cheating, forgery and using a forged document. The Insurance Act, 1938 and the IRDAI regulations allow an insurer to avoid a policy obtained by fraud and to recover a fraudulent claim. The insurer can also report the matter to the police. A surveyor or repairer who issues a false report can be liable as an abettor. A staged collision can also be an offence under the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and the BNS.
9-21.cost: No cost. Report the loss truthfully and keep the photographs, the FIR and the repair estimate. Do not accept an offer to 'adjust' the bill.
9-21.caveats: A genuine claim that is poorly documented can look exaggerated; keep the evidence. A minor dent that is repaired later is not fraud, but attributing old damage to a new incident is. Health-insurance misuse of a family member's card is also fraud.
9-21.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Insurance Act, 1938. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>; Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>

9-22.title: Do not sell an organ or recruit a donor for money — the Transplantation of Human Organs Act prohibits it
9-22.inPlainWords: The Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, 1994 prohibits the purchase or sale of human organs and commercial dealing in them. A living donor must be a near relative or a person approved by an authorisation committee for special reasons, and the donation must be voluntary and unpaid. Recruiting a donor for money can lead to imprisonment and a fine, and the transplant centre can lose its registration.
9-22.benefit: The 1994 Act, as amended in 2011, regulates the removal, storage and transplantation of organs. Commercial dealing is punishable with imprisonment and a fine, and the Act provides for the registration of transplant centres and the approval of living donors by an authorisation committee. The BNS, 2023 can also apply to cheating, hurt or trafficking. A doctor who removes an organ without the required consent or committee approval commits an offence.
9-22.cost: No cost. A lawful living donation goes through a registered hospital and the authorisation committee, without payment. A patient should register on the national transplant waiting list.
9-22.caveats: A 'donation' in exchange for money, a job or a visa is commercial dealing. A foreign donor needs additional clearance. Post-mortem donation is a separate, voluntary process. If you are in financial distress, use the welfare routes in Section 7 rather than a broker.
9-22.sources: Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act, 1994. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation. <https://notto.mohfw.gov.in/>; Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. <https://mohfw.gov.in/>

9-23.title: Prostitution is not licensed in India; keeping a brothel or soliciting in public is an offence
9-23.inPlainWords: The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 punishes keeping a brothel, living on the earnings of prostitution, soliciting in a public place and trafficking for prostitution. The BNS, 2023 and the IT Act cover related offences. A person who is exploited can be treated as a victim and referred to a shelter, while the organiser faces a criminal case. Do not organise, rent a place for, or advertise sexual services.
9-23.benefit: The 1956 Act provides imprisonment and fines for keeping or managing a brothel, for living wholly or partly on the earnings of prostitution, and for soliciting. The BNS, 2023 contains offences for trafficking and sexual exploitation. The IT Act covers online solicitation. A hotel or landlord who knowingly allows the activity can be liable. The Act also provides for the rescue and rehabilitation of victims.
9-23.cost: No cost. Do not rent a premises for the activity, do not advertise it, and do not act as an intermediary.
9-23.caveats: The law distinguishes the person exploited from the organiser; a victim should not be treated as the accused. Health services and HIV prevention are available without judgment. If you are being coerced, contact the police or a shelter.
9-23.sources: Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Women and Child Development. <https://wcd.gov.in/>

9-24.title: Fan translation, re-hosting films and sharing pirated books infringe copyright even if you charge nothing
9-24.inPlainWords: Translating a book or comic and posting it without permission, or uploading a film or e-book to a public drive, infringes copyright. The Copyright Act, 1957 gives the owner the rights of translation, reproduction and communication to the public. Civil remedies include an injunction and damages; commercial-scale infringement can be a criminal offence. Do not run a resource-sharing portal or an ad-supported download channel.
9-24.benefit: The Copyright Act, 1957 provides civil remedies and criminal punishment for infringement. The fair-dealing exception for private study, research, criticism or review does not cover publishing a translation or a full copy online. The court can award damages, costs and an injunction, and can order the material to be taken down. The IT Act, 2000 and the intermediary rules provide a notice-and-takedown route for a host.
9-24.cost: No cost to stop. Buy or license the work, or keep the translation private. If you run a site, publish a clear takedown policy and act on notices.
9-24.caveats: A short quotation for criticism may be fair dealing; a full translation is not. A non-commercial motive does not make the copy lawful, though it affects the remedy. A platform that ignores a takedown notice can lose its safe harbour.
9-24.sources: Copyright Act, 1957. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Information Technology Act, 2000. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Intellectual Property India. <https://ipindia.gov.in/>

9-25.title: Get a licence before you publish or sell fan fiction, or replace the borrowed characters with original ones
9-25.inPlainWords: Fan fiction that borrows a character, a fictional world or a distinctive plot can infringe copyright, and selling it can also be passing off or unfair competition. The Copyright Act, 1957 protects the expression, not the abstract idea. A free, non-commercial story is lower risk but not automatically lawful. If you want to publish or sell, get a written licence or create original characters and settings.
9-25.benefit: The Copyright Act, 1957 gives the author the exclusive right to reproduce, adapt and communicate the work. A derivative work needs a licence unless it falls within fair dealing. The Trademarks Act, 1999 and the common-law action for passing off can apply where the marketing uses the original title or characters. The court can grant an injunction, damages and costs. A publisher or platform may also require an indemnity.
9-25.cost: A licence or an original rewrite costs time and money, but less than litigation. Keep the licence and the correspondence. If you cannot get a licence, change the names, the relationships and the distinctive world.
9-25.caveats: The line between an unprotected idea and protected expression is decided case by case. A parody may be protected, but commercial exploitation is riskier. A publisher's contract can assign the rights, so an author may not be free to license a sequel.
9-25.sources: Copyright Act, 1957. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Trademarks Act, 1999. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Intellectual Property India. <https://ipindia.gov.in/>

9-26.title: Do not carry a baton, stun gun, dagger or pepper spray as a self-defence shortcut; check the Arms Act and state rules
9-26.inPlainWords: The Arms Act, 1959 and the state police rules regulate the possession and carrying of many weapons, including daggers, spring knives, batons and stun guns. Carrying a prohibited weapon in public can lead to arrest and a criminal case, even if you never use it. A weapon also escalates a fight. Keep distance, call 112, and use force only if the law allows it.
9-26.benefit: The Arms Act, 1959 and the Arms Rules, 2016 set the categories and the licences. The BNS, 2023 contains offences for criminal intimidation, hurt and attempt. The right of private defence under the BNS is limited to the force necessary to repel the threat; a concealed weapon can turn a lawful defence into excessive force. Pepper spray is legal in some states and restricted in others; check the local police rules.
9-26.cost: No cost. Do not buy a prohibited weapon. If your work puts you at risk, ask for security, change the route and keep the police helpline on speed dial.
9-26.caveats: A household knife in the kitchen is not the same as a dagger carried in public. A licensed weapon is still subject to the licence conditions. If you have already been charged, take a criminal lawyer immediately.
9-26.sources: Arms Act, 1959. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (private defence). <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of Home Affairs. <https://www.mha.gov.in/>

9-27.title: Do not fish in a closed season or sanctuary, and never use electric current, poison or explosives
9-27.inPlainWords: State fisheries laws and the Indian Fisheries Act, 1897 prohibit destructive fishing, and the Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 protects scheduled aquatic species. Using electric current, poison or explosives is an offence and can attract imprisonment and a fine. A closed season protects breeding, and a sanctuary is closed to fishing. Check the state fisheries department notice before you set out.
9-27.benefit: The Indian Fisheries Act, 1897 and the state fisheries Acts restrict the use of dynamite, poison and fixed nets. The Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972 protects scheduled fish and other aquatic species and punishes their capture or trade. The BNS, 2023 can apply where an explosion endangers life. A boat, net or equipment used in the offence can be seized.
9-27.cost: No cost. Check the state fisheries notification for the closed season and the permitted gear. A licence may be required for commercial fishing.
9-27.caveats: Recreational angling rules differ by state and by reservoir. A catch from a protected species must be released. Do not buy fish you know were caught illegally; that can be handling stolen property or a wildlife offence.
9-27.sources: Indian Fisheries Act, 1897. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Fisheries. <https://dof.gov.in/>

9-28.title: Never light a fire in a forest or grassland fire-prevention zone; report a wildfire at once on 112
9-28.inPlainWords: Lighting a fire, burning stubble or leaving a cigarette in a forest or grassland during the fire season is an offence under the Indian Forest Act, 1927 and the state forest rules, and can lead to a criminal case if it spreads. The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 and the National Disaster Management Authority guidelines add restrictions. Call 112 or the forest department immediately if you see a fire; do not wait.
9-28.benefit: The Indian Forest Act, 1927 punishes setting fire to a forest, and the state forest Acts add penalties. The BNS, 2023 contains offences for mischief and for rash or negligent acts endangering life. The National Disaster Management Authority and the forest department run fire-response systems; a quick report can save lives and land. A person who causes a fire can be liable for the cost of extinguishing it and for reforestation.
9-28.cost: No cost. Use flowers or a plant instead of burning paper at a grave. Do not burn stubble or weeds in dry weather. Carry out cigarette butts.
9-28.caveats: A small controlled fire can become a crown fire in minutes. A fire lit on private land can still spread to forest land. Do not try to fight a large fire yourself; call the professionals and move upwind.
9-28.sources: Indian Forest Act, 1927. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Disaster Management Authority. <https://ndma.gov.in/>; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. <https://moef.gov.in/>

9-29.title: Never sit an exam for someone else or buy answers; the Public Examinations Act, 2024 makes it a criminal offence
9-29.inPlainWords: The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024 punishes impersonation, leaking a paper, buying or selling answers and organising cheating in a public examination. The BNS, 2023 also covers cheating and forgery. A conviction can mean imprisonment and a fine, and the candidate can be barred from future exams. A few marks are not worth a criminal record.
9-29.benefit: The 2024 Act covers public examinations conducted by the central government and listed authorities, and provides imprisonment and fines for unfair means, including impersonation and collusion by a service provider. The BNS, 2023 covers cheating, forgery and criminal conspiracy. The exam authority can cancel the result and debar the candidate. A coaching centre or invigilator who organises the cheating can be prosecuted.
9-29.cost: No cost. Prepare and sit the exam yourself. If you are offered a 'guaranteed' paper, report it to the exam authority and the police.
9-29.caveats: The Act's coverage depends on the examination and the authority; state examinations have their own laws. A leaked paper is evidence; do not share it. If you are caught, take a lawyer before making a statement.
9-29.sources: Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Union Public Service Commission. <https://upsc.gov.in/>
